images.title: Ways to describe a data set
images.purpose: Show on one small bar graph the maximum, the minimum, the range and the mean of a data set, the measures used to compare the onion prices.
images.composition: One short bar graph of 5 bars sits in the centre left with generous white space; a range bracket stands at its right and one mean line runs across it.
exact_structure: 5 vertical bars of equal width with equal gaps, standing on one dark grey (#2B2B2B) baseline, left to right with heights 20, 24, 18, 30 and 28 units drawn to scale.
The bars of height 20, 24 and 28 are teal (#0072B2); the tallest bar (30) is green (#009E73); the shortest bar (18) is vermilion (#D55E00).
Each bar carries its value printed just above its top: 20, 24, 18, 30, 28.
A small label Maximum sits beside the top of the green bar and a small label Minimum beside the top of the vermilion bar.
A grey (#6B7280) dashed horizontal line runs across all 5 bars at height 24, labelled Mean = 120 ÷ 5 = 24 at its right end.
To the right of the bars a reddish purple (#CC79A7) vertical bracket spans from height 18 to height 30, labelled Range = 30 − 18 = 12.
No axis numbers, no month names, no title text in the frame.
rejection: a number of bars other than 5
the mean line drawn at a height other than 24
the range bracket not running from 18 to 30
the green and vermilion bars swapped
images.takeaway: One data set can be described by its maximum, minimum, range and mean, and each tells a different thing.
images.description: A bar graph of 5 bars with heights 20, 24, 18, 30 and 28, the tallest green, the shortest vermilion, a dashed mean line at 24 and a range bracket from 18 to 30.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text and video for this concept.
images.teaching_notes: Point to each measure in turn and ask which one Khushboo, Nafisa and Jithin each used for the onions.

image_decisions.why: Seeing the maximum, minimum, range and mean on one picture separates the different ways of comparing data.
